prompt: Which experiments confirmed de Broglie's idea that electrons behave as waves?

choices.text: Electron diffraction by Davisson and Germer, and by G.P. Thomson, in 1927
Millikan's photoelectric experiments
choices.why: Millikan's experiments confirmed Einstein's photon picture of light, not the wave nature of electrons.

choices.text: The gold-foil scattering experiments of Geiger and Marsden
choices.why: Those showed that atoms have a small, heavy nucleus. Electron diffraction showed electrons behave as waves.

choices.text: Young's double-slit experiment of 1801
choices.why: Young's experiment showed that light behaves as a wave, more than a century before electron diffraction.

explanation: De Broglie's proposal was confirmed by the electron diffraction experiments of G.P. Thomson and of C. Davisson and L. H. Germer in 1927: electrons scattered from atoms in a crystal produced an interference pattern.

prompt: When does diffraction happen?

choices.text: When waves meet obstacles or gaps of a size comparable to their wavelength
Only when light passes through glass
choices.why: Diffraction happens for any waves, including electrons and neutrons, when the obstacles are comparable to the wavelength.

choices.text: Only for very slow particles
choices.why: What matters is that the wavelength is comparable to the spacing of the obstacles.

choices.text: Whenever a particle is charged
choices.why: Neutrons, which have no charge, diffract too. The condition is about wavelength and spacing.

explanation: Diffraction occurs when waves encounter obstacles whose size is comparable with their wavelength. Diffraction patterns are obtained if the wavelength is comparable to the spacing between scattering centers.

prompt: Which phenomenon is the main way to identify wave behavior?

choices.text: Interference
Reflection
choices.why: Particles bounce off surfaces too. Interference, where waves add up or cancel, is the main sign of a wave.

choices.text: Absorption
choices.why: Particles can be absorbed too. Interference is the main sign of wave behavior.

choices.text: Moving in a straight line
choices.why: That is what classical particles do. Interference is the sign of a wave.

explanation: Interference, in which two or more waves superimpose to form a resultant wave of greater or lower amplitude, is the primary property used to identify wave behavior.

prompt: What did Thomas Young's double-slit experiment of 1801 demonstrate?

choices.text: That light behaves as a wave
That electrons behave as waves
choices.why: Electron diffraction came in 1927. Young's experiment of 1801 was done with light.

choices.text: That light is made of particles called photons
choices.why: Young's bright and dark fringes showed the wave behavior of light.

choices.text: That atoms have a nucleus
choices.why: That came from the gold-foil experiments. Young's experiment showed light behaving as a wave.

explanation: Thomas Young first performed the double-slit experiment in 1801 as a demonstration of the wave behavior of light: light passing through two slits produces bright and dark interference fringes.

prompt: Why can an electron microscope show much smaller objects than a light microscope?

choices.text: The wavelength of its electrons can be up to 100,000 times shorter than that of visible light
Electrons are larger than photons
choices.why: It is about wavelength: the electrons' wavelength is much shorter than visible light's, so they resolve smaller details.

choices.text: Electrons travel faster than light
choices.why: Nothing travels faster than light. The electrons' much shorter wavelength is what gives the better resolution.

choices.text: Electron microscopes use a brighter lamp
choices.why: They use a beam of electrons instead of light, and the electrons' short wavelength gives the better resolution.

explanation: An electron microscope uses a beam of accelerated electrons. Their wavelength can be up to 100,000 times shorter than visible light's, so it reaches better than 50 pm resolution, against about 200 nm for most light microscopes.

prompt: Roughly what wavelength do neutrons need for neutron diffraction from a solid?

choices.text: About 0.1 nm, the typical spacing between atoms
About 500 nm, like visible light
choices.why: That is far larger than the spacing between atoms. The wavelength must be near 0.1 nm.

choices.text: About 1 m
choices.why: Diffraction needs a wavelength comparable to the spacing between atoms, about 0.1 nm.

choices.text: Any wavelength works
choices.why: Diffraction needs a wavelength comparable to the spacing of the obstacles, here about 0.1 nm.

explanation: When neutrons from a reactor are slowed down and selected by speed, their wavelength is near one angstrom (0.1 nm), the typical separation between atoms in a solid, so they can be diffracted.

prompt: What does a moderator, such as graphite, do for neutron diffraction?

choices.text: It slows down fast neutrons, so that their wavelengths become comparable to atomic spacing
It speeds the neutrons up
choices.why: Fast neutrons have wavelengths that are too short. The moderator slows them down to make their wavelengths longer.

choices.text: It gives the neutrons an electric charge
choices.why: Neutrons have no charge. The moderator just slows them down.

choices.text: It absorbs all the neutrons
choices.why: Neutrons can penetrate the moderator; it slows them down rather than stopping them all.

explanation: Neutrons released in fission are fast, and their wavelengths are much smaller than atomic dimensions. A moderator such as graphite slows them down appreciably, giving them longer wavelengths useful for diffraction.

prompt: According to the section, is an electron a particle or a wave?

choices.text: Neither: particle and wave are two models, each useful in different situations
Always a particle
choices.why: Electrons diffract and interfere like waves, so a particle model alone is not enough.

choices.text: Always a wave
choices.why: Electrons are detected at single points, like particles, so a wave model alone is not enough.

choices.text: A particle on weekdays and a wave at weekends
choices.why: Which model you use depends on the calculation, not on the day.

explanation: An electron is neither a particle nor a wave. Describing it as a particle is a model that works well in some circumstances, and describing it as a wave is another model that works well in others.

prompt: The interference pattern made by electrons scattered from a crystal looked just like the pattern made by what?

choices.text: Water waves passing through two holes in a barrier
Bullets fired at a wall with two windows
choices.why: Bullets are classical particles, so they leave two separate bands of hits with no bright and dark pattern.

choices.text: Sand poured through two holes in a sheet
choices.why: Sand grains are classical particles that pile up behind each hole. The electron pattern matched waves that interfere.

choices.text: Light bouncing off a flat mirror
choices.why: Reflection from a mirror does not make bright and dark fringes. The electron pattern matched water waves that pass through two holes and interfere.

explanation: In the 1927 electron diffraction experiments, the scattered electrons produced an interference pattern just like the one made when water waves pass through two holes in a barrier and the separate wave fronts combine and interfere.

prompt: According to the section, which technology works by the diffraction and interference of light?

choices.text: Holography
Incandescent light bulbs
choices.why: A bulb glows because its filament is hot, like a blackbody. Holography is the example that uses diffracted light interfering.

choices.text: Photocells that use the photoelectric effect
choices.why: The photoelectric effect shows light acting as particles (photons). Holography relies on light's wave behavior.

choices.text: Radio transmitters
choices.why: A transmitter sends out radiation from electrons driven up and down a wire. Holography is the example of light diffraction.

explanation: Light diffracts around objects, giving an interference pattern particular to the object. In holography, the diffracted light is allowed to interfere with the original beam, and the hologram is viewed by shining the original beam on the image.

prompt: In Young's double-slit experiment, what does each of the two slits act as?

choices.text: A point source of spherical waves
A mirror that sends the light back
choices.why: The light passes through the slits. Each slit becomes a source of spherical waves, and the two sets of waves interfere.

choices.text: A filter that lets through only one color
choices.why: The slits do not sort colors. Each one acts as a point source of waves that then interfere with the waves from the other slit.

choices.text: A lens that focuses the light to one spot
choices.why: The slits spread the light out rather than focus it. Each slit is a point source of spherical waves.

explanation: Plane light waves fall on the two slits. Each slit then becomes a point source of spherical waves, and these waves interfere with each other to give the light and dark fringes on the screen.

prompt: According to classical physics, what should a beam of electrons fired through two slits produce on a detector?

choices.text: Two bands of hits, one behind each slit
Many bright and dark interference bands
choices.why: That is what is really seen when the slits are small and close together. Classical particles travel in straight lines and would give just two bands.

choices.text: One band of hits midway between the slits
choices.why: Classical particles go straight through each slit, so they land behind the slits, like bullets through two windows.

choices.text: No hits at all, because electrons cannot pass through slits
choices.why: Classically, electrons that pass through a slit travel on in a straight line and hit the detector behind it.

explanation: Classically, electrons travel in straight lines, so firing them through two slits should give two bands of hits, like a machine gun fired at a house with two windows. Instead, with small, close slits, electrons diffract and interfere like waves.

prompt: In the double-slit experiment with light, how is the light detected at the screen?

choices.text: As individual hits at discrete points
As a smooth wave spread evenly over the screen
choices.why: The light is always absorbed at discrete points, like particles. The pattern shows up in how densely the hits fall.

choices.text: Only at two spots, one behind each slit
choices.why: That is what classical particles would give. Light gives bright and dark bands, built up from many individual hits.

choices.text: As one flash that covers the whole screen at once
choices.why: The light arrives as separate hits at single points. The bright and dark bands come from where the hits are dense or sparse.

explanation: Light is always absorbed at the screen at discrete points, as individual particles. The interference pattern appears through the varying density of these hits: many where the bands are bright and few where they are dark.

prompt: When detectors are placed at the slits of a double-slit experiment with light, what is found for each photon?

choices.text: It passes through only one of the slits
It passes through both slits at once
choices.why: That is what a wave would do. The detectors find each photon going through one slit, as a classical particle would.

choices.text: It splits into two photons, one for each slit
choices.why: Photons are not split by the slits. Each detected photon passes through one slit only.

choices.text: It passes through neither slit
choices.why: Photons that reach the screen do go through the slits. Detectors show that each one goes through just one slit.

explanation: Versions of the experiment with detectors at the slits find that each detected photon passes through one slit, as a classical particle would, and not through both slits, as a wave would. Light shows both particle and wave behavior.

prompt: What must be done to see electrons fired at a double slit interfere like waves?

choices.text: Make the slits small enough and close enough together
Make the slits wide and far apart
choices.why: Wide, distant slits just give two bands of hits. Diffraction needs slits and spacings comparable to the electrons' wavelength.

choices.text: Speed the electrons up as much as possible
choices.why: Faster electrons have more momentum and so a shorter wavelength, which makes diffraction harder to see. What matters is small, close slits.

choices.text: Bend the electron beam with a magnetic field
choices.why: A magnetic field only curves the electrons' paths. Interference shows up when the slits are small and close together.

explanation: If the slits are made small enough and close enough together, electrons diffract through the slits and interfere just like waves. Diffraction needs obstacles comparable in size to the wavelength.

prompt: The photoelectric effect demonstrated the particle nature of light. What did the Davisson–Germer experiment demonstrate?

choices.text: The wave nature of matter
The particle nature of matter
choices.why: Matter acting as particles was the classical picture already. Electron diffraction showed that matter also behaves as waves.

choices.text: The wave nature of light
choices.why: That was shown in 1801 by Young's double-slit experiment. Davisson and Germer showed that electrons, which are matter, behave as waves.

choices.text: That atoms have a small, heavy nucleus
choices.why: That came from α-particle scattering. The Davisson–Germer experiment showed the wave nature of matter.

explanation: Just as the photoelectric effect demonstrated the particle nature of light, the Davisson–Germer experiment showed the wave nature of matter. Together they completed the picture of wave-particle duality.

prompt: Why was the discovery that electrons behave as waves so important to physicists?

choices.text: Wave equations could now describe matter, using the de Broglie wavelength
It showed that electrons have no mass
choices.why: Electrons do have mass. The result meant matter has a wavelength, so wave equations could be used for it.

choices.text: It showed that only electrons can act as waves
choices.why: It meant the opposite: any particle could show wave behavior. Neutrons diffract too.

choices.text: It proved that classical physics works for electrons
choices.why: Classical physics predicts no electron interference. The result showed matter must also be treated with wave equations.

explanation: The result meant that any particle could show wave characteristics, and that wave equations could be used to describe matter if one used the de Broglie wavelength. It was a pivotal step in the development of quantum mechanics.

prompt: What limits most light microscopes to a resolution of about 200 nm?

choices.text: Diffraction of the visible light they use
The brightness of the lamp
choices.why: A brighter lamp does not help. The light's wavelength makes it diffract, and that blurs details smaller than about 200 nm.

choices.text: The quality of the glass in the lenses
choices.why: Even perfect lenses cannot get past this limit. It comes from the diffraction of visible light.

choices.text: The speed of light
choices.why: Speed is not the issue. Visible light's wavelength is long, so it diffracts and limits the resolution.

explanation: Most light microscopes are limited by diffraction to about 200 nm resolution. Electrons can have wavelengths up to 100,000 times shorter, so electron microscopes can resolve much smaller details.

prompt: Why can neutrons pass through about 10 cm of lead?

choices.text: They have no electric charge, so they don't interact with the atoms' electrons
They are much lighter than electrons
choices.why: A neutron (1.67 × 10^−27 kg) is far heavier than an electron. Neutrons penetrate because they have no charge.

choices.text: They travel faster than light
choices.why: Nothing travels faster than light. Neutrons penetrate because, with no charge, they ignore the atoms' electrons.

choices.text: They are waves with no mass
choices.why: Neutrons have mass, about 1.67 × 10^−27 kg. They are penetrating because they carry no electric charge.

explanation: Neutrons have no electric charge, so they do not interact with the atomic electrons. That makes them very penetrating, typically about 10 cm in lead, and they interact directly with the nuclei instead.

prompt: In neutron diffraction, why do ordinary hydrogen and deuterium contribute differently to the diffracted intensity?

choices.text: Neutrons interact with the nucleus, and the effect depends on the isotope
Deuterium has more electrons than hydrogen
choices.why: Both have one electron. Neutrons interact with the nucleus, which differs between the two isotopes.

choices.text: Deuterium has a larger nuclear charge
choices.why: Both nuclei have one proton and the same charge. Neutrons interact directly with the nucleus, and each isotope contributes differently.

choices.text: Neutrons interact only with an atom's electrons
choices.why: It is the reverse: neutrons have no charge and ignore the electrons. They interact directly with the nucleus.

explanation: Neutrons interact directly with the nucleus of the atom, and the contribution to the diffracted intensity depends on each isotope. So regular hydrogen and deuterium, which have the same electrons but different nuclei, contribute differently.

prompt: In neutron diffraction, how do light (low Z) atoms often compare with heavy (large Z) atoms?

choices.text: Light atoms can still contribute strongly to the diffracted intensity
Light atoms cannot be seen when heavy atoms are present
choices.why: The section says light atoms often contribute strongly even in the presence of large Z atoms.

choices.text: Only atoms heavier than lead can diffract neutrons
choices.why: Atoms or their nuclei of any kind can serve as diffraction obstacles, and light atoms often contribute strongly.

choices.text: Light atoms absorb all the neutrons that reach them
choices.why: Light atoms scatter neutrons and contribute strongly to the diffraction pattern rather than simply absorbing them.

explanation: Because neutrons interact with nuclei rather than electrons, light (low Z) atoms often contribute strongly to the diffracted intensity even in the presence of large Z atoms.

prompt: In what year was neutron diffraction proposed, to make use of de Broglie's idea that matter has wave properties?

choices.why: 1801 is when Thomas Young did his double-slit experiment with light. Neutron diffraction was proposed in 1934.
1913 is the year of Bohr's model of the atom. Neutron diffraction was proposed in 1934.
1927 is when Davisson and Germer, and G.P. Thomson, reported electron diffraction. Neutron diffraction was proposed later, in 1934.

explanation: Neutron diffraction was proposed in 1934 to exploit de Broglie's hypothesis about the wave nature of matter, a few years after electron diffraction was observed in 1927.

prompt: What happens in interference?

choices.text: Waves combine to give a bigger or smaller amplitude
A wave bounces back off a surface
choices.why: That is reflection. In interference, two or more waves superimpose to give a wave of greater or lower amplitude.

choices.text: A wave bends as it enters a new material
choices.why: That is refraction. Interference is two or more waves adding together, making the amplitude larger or smaller.

choices.text: A wave slowly fades as it travels
choices.why: That is the wave losing energy. Interference is waves superimposing to give a resultant wave of greater or lower amplitude.

explanation: Interference is a wave phenomenon in which two or more waves superimpose to form a resultant wave of greater or lower amplitude. Where they add up you get bright bands, and where they cancel you get dark bands.

prompt: Use p = h/λ with h = 6.6 × 10^−34 J·s. What is the momentum, in kg·m/s, of a neutron whose wavelength is 1.8 × 10^−10 m, about the spacing between atoms? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e-19.)
Use KE = p^2/(2m). What is the kinetic energy, in J, of a neutron (m = 1.67 × 10^−27 kg) with momentum p = 3.7 × 10^−24 kg·m/s? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e-19.)
explanation: p^2 = (3.7 × 10^−24)^2 = 1.37 × 10^−47, so KE = (1.37 × 10^−47)/(2 × 1.67 × 10^−27) J = 4.1 × 10^−21 J. Neutrons from nuclear fission are much more energetic than this.

prompt: The electrons in an electron microscope can have a wavelength up to 100,000 times shorter than visible light. What is a wavelength 100,000 times shorter than 500 nm, in pm? (1 nm = 1000 pm.)
explanation: 500 nm/100,000 = 0.005 nm = 5 pm. Such short wavelengths are why electron microscopes resolve far smaller details than light microscopes.

prompt: A transmission electron microscope can magnify up to about 10,000,000 times, while a light microscope's useful magnification tops out near 2000 times. How many times greater is the electron microscope's maximum magnification?
explanation: 10,000,000/2000 = 5000. The electron microscope's much shorter wavelength lets it magnify about 5000 times more usefully.

prompt: Use λ = h/(mv) with h = 6.6 × 10^−34 J·s. A neutron (m = 1.67 × 10^−27 kg) has been slowed to 4000 m/s. What is its de Broglie wavelength, in nm?
explanation: mv = (1.67 × 10^−27 kg)(4000 m/s) = 6.68 × 10^−24 kg·m/s, so λ = (6.6 × 10^−34)/(6.68 × 10^−24) m = 9.9 × 10^−11 m ≈ 0.099 nm. That is about one angstrom, the spacing between atoms in a solid, so these slowed neutrons can be diffracted.
